title: Celsius's scale was upside down
hook: In the first Celsius scale, water boiled at 0 and froze at 100.
peek: When the Swedish astronomer Anders Celsius proposed his temperature scale in 1742, it ran the opposite way from the one we use. Hotter meant a lower number. Someone flipped it soon after he died, and historians still argue about who.
lede: In 1742 Anders Celsius, an astronomer at Uppsala in Sweden, presented a paper to the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences describing a thermometer with 100 steps between two fixed points. He put 0 at the boiling point of water and 100 at the freezing point. On his scale a cold Swedish winter day would have read well above 100 degrees.

bullets.text: Celsius showed that melting snow gives the same reading whatever the latitude or air pressure, making it a reliable fixed point. He also found that the boiling point does change with pressure, so he specified a standard pressure for it.

The scale was turned the right way up around 1744 to 1745, shortly after Celsius died. Credit is often given to the botanist Carl Linnaeus, who ordered a flipped thermometer for his greenhouse, but others name instrument makers or colleagues at Uppsala.
In 1743 the French scientist Jean-Pierre Christin independently proposed a scale with 0 for freezing and 100 for boiling. For a time it was known in France as the Lyon thermometer.
For two centuries the scale was widely called centigrade, meaning a hundred steps. In 1948 an international conference on weights and measures officially renamed it after Celsius.
